_provenance.audit: 10_access_publishing/governance_audit_data.json -> audit_log.events (verbatim, HTML stripped) and model_rules (as policies). Stats computed from the Table Catalog PII/review columns and the six cost caps -- none typed
_provenance.traces: 10_access_publishing/governance_audit_data.json -> sealed_traces[11]. p50/p95 and the cost total are computed from those eleven; the waterfall is the longest trace's own steps[]
_provenance.evals: DERIVED, not carried: the package ships no eval-run artifact. Runs and checks are computed from 05_knowledge_graph/graph_studio.json (sanity_checks, review_queue, lanes) and 06_queries/query_set.json (confidence distribution, decline count). No number here is typed
_provenance.change_signals: 05_knowledge_graph/knowledge_graph.json -> gaps[]. The "action" field carries the gap's own do_not clause, because the useful instruction here is what not to do
_provenance.column_profiles: 02_profiling/Metadata_Profiling.xlsx -> the three per-surface profile sheets, read cell by cell
_provenance.column_vocabulary: the 50 highest-confidence columns across the two profiled structured views
_provenance.drives: _build/contracts.json (the contract extraction of the five folders in 08_unstructured); folder totals are the extraction's own awarded/adjusted figures
_provenance.drive_credentials: one handle per drive; deterministic md5
_provenance.document_extractions: 08_unstructured/Entity_Extraction_Map.xlsx -> 'Extracted Entities' sheet, one entry per extracted entity (423), joined to the Documents sheet for the project code and to 07_reports/report_data.json -> projects[] for the facility and state. linked_manifests is computed: how many documents in the corpus resolve to the same graph node
_provenance.graph_domains: 07_reports/report_data.json -> tenant.domainPack for the two bound domains; the two unmet domains are the graph's own gaps[] stated as unmet fit
_provenance.graph_studio: 05_knowledge_graph/graph_studio.json (review_queue, lanes, sanity_checks) and knowledge_graph.json (442 nodes, 908 edges). Canvas x/y is a deterministic radial layout computed here -- presentation, not data
_provenance.graph_personas: 06_queries/query_set.json -> counts.by_persona (the seven personas the query set actually asks as), ordered by how many questions each asks
_provenance.graph_answer_formats: the block mixes the query set actually uses (chart+metric+table+text, chart+metric+text, chart+table+text, metric+table+text, metric+text, text), named as formats
_provenance.graph_use_cases: the one use case this package is built around; personas, KPIs, hero questions and gap decisions are all read out of the artifacts above rather than restated
_provenance.graph_use_case_templates: assembled from the ids emitted above; no free text beyond the description
_provenance.ask_answers: 06_queries/query_set.json -> queries[40]. Field renames only: id->answer_id, type->kind, response.summary->summary, response.blocks->blocks, confidence{level,score}->confidence_level+confidence. Block bodies are byte-identical
_provenance.whatif: 09_What if lens/whatif_capex_data.json and whatif_publish_access_data.json, both of which were themselves extracted from the built page at runtime, mapped onto the VLS whatif key set. headroom is COMPUTED per lever from (envelope - base forecast) and asserted against the screen's own worked example. The three candidate-pool keys are empty by design -- the CAPEX lens moves continuous levers, not swappable candidates; see _not_applicable
_provenance.reports: 07_reports/report_specs.json + report_resolved.json for the three published reports (tiles are the reports' own figure rows, footer their own caveats), report_authoring_data.json for the authoring surface, report_data.json for the measure catalogue and the spine tables, and governance_audit_data.json for the two gates, the published-artifact register and the reader directory

graph_metrics.name: Overrun amount
graph_metrics.definition:
Overrun Amount =
VAR ExceptionCategories =
    { "Network blankets", "Lead Capex Budget Category", "Meter blankets", "Plant roll-up" }
VAR ExceptionActuals =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( 'EPBCS_DATA_2'[FY26 YearTotal Actual] ),
        KEEPFILTERS ( 'EPBCS_DATA_2'[Budget Category] IN ExceptionCategories )
    )
VAR StandardActuals =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( 'EPBCS_DATA_2'[Inception to Date (ITD) Actuals] ),
        KEEPFILTERS ( NOT ( 'EPBCS_DATA_2'[Budget Category] IN ExceptionCategories ) )
    )
RETURN
    ExceptionActuals + StandardActuals
        - SUM ( 'EPBCS_DATA_2'[Most Recent Budget Plan in PeopleSoft (Value)] )

columns.description: Spend category, using the same 6-value vocabulary as Projects.'Budget Category': Plant large projects (1,711), PFAS (635), Network blankets (619), Lead Capex Budget Category (398), Overhead - Budget Category (204), Network common projects (203).

Projected date the asset enters service. NULL on 770 of 3,770 rows, and 2026-01-01 on 693 more, which reads as a placeholder rather than a real estimate. Same measure as Projects.'Estimated In Service Date'. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
How the in-service date is derived: 'Date' (2,435 rows) or 'Monthly' (1,335). Source header was 'in_service_method'.
Constant 2026-12-31 on all 3,770 rows, so it carries no per-project information in this extract. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.

Flag whose column in the source file was headed 'NEEDS TO BE UPDATED' -- a working note left by the author, not a real field name. FALSE on 2,955 rows, TRUE on 815. The condition it flags is undocumented, so treat both name and meaning as provisional.

Capital project this in-service record belongs to. 3,770 distinct values, one row per project. Joins to Projects.'Project Code' -- but 260 of them have NO matching row in Projects (mostly older C21B* codes), so an inner join silently drops them. Use a LEFT join, or filter, deliberately.
Value of this change order in US dollars. Negative amounts are credits; the source file wrote them in parentheses. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.

Free-text justification for the change order, extracted from the source contract document: differing site conditions, owner-caused delay, quantity reconciliation or negotiated credits. Header in the source file read 'Basis (extracted narrative)'.
Sequential change-order number within its contract, CO-001 through CO-006. Unique only in combination with Contract ID.
Identifier of the contract this change order amends (e.g. QDN-2025-C01, DEF-2023-C01). Joins to Contracts.'Contract ID'. 16 distinct contracts across the 22 change orders; no orphans.
Calendar days added to the Contract Times by this change order. 18 of 22 rows are 0; the non-zero values are 31, 118, 214 and 274.
Capital project the amended contract belongs to. Five values: C23B225_690, C25B315_658, CZZF50229_623, CZZF5034_698, C25B175_675. Joins to Projects.'Project Code'.
Contract price once this change order is applied. The final value per contract reconciles to Contracts.'Price As Adjusted USD'. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
Count of executed change orders on the contract: 0 (15 rows), 1 (12), 2 (3) and 4 (1). Verified to match the rows actually present in CAPEX.Change_Orders for all 31 contracts.

Unique identifier of the contract, one per row (31 contracts). Most follow <project>-<year>-<letter><nn>, the letter marking the instrument: C construction, E engineering, S supply, P professional services, R restoration, T trenchless. Several do not (WLR-25-2, WM-23-A, WM-26-B). Parent key for Change_Orders.'Contract ID'; every change order resolves to a contract here.
The contracting firm on the other side of the agreement: contractor, engineer, supplier or testing laboratory. 24 distinct firms across the 31 contracts; some hold more than one.
The standard EJCDC document the instrument is based on: E-500 (13 rows), C-521 (12), C-520 (2), and the literal 'Supply agreement (no EJCDC form)' (4) where none applies.
Date the contract was signed. Values span 2022 to 2026. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load. The original held this as text ('15 September 2025').

The kind of agreement. 16 distinct values including Construction Agreement, Owner-Engineer Agreement, Construction Management Agreement, Quality Assurance Agreement, Equipment Supply Agreement and LSLR Unit Price Agreement.

Cumulative value of change orders against the contract, i.e. Price As Adjusted USD minus Price At Award USD. Negative values are net credits. NULL on the 15 contracts with no change orders (the source wrote a literal '-'). Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
Current contract price after all executed change orders. Equals Price At Award USD on the 15 contracts with no change orders. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
Original contract price at execution, in US dollars. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.

Human-readable project name, one-to-one with Project Code. Five values: Quarrydown WTP PFAS Treatment, Redmont Well Field Expansion, Dunmoor East Filter Media Renewal, Westbrook Lead Service Line Replacement, Selby Point Trunk Main Rehabilitation.
Capital project the contract belongs to. Five values: C23B225_690, CZZF50229_623, C25B175_675, CZZF5034_698, C25B315_658. Joins to Projects.'Project Code'.
Filename of the PDF this contract record was extracted from, e.g. 'QDN-2025-C01_Construction_Agreement_Kelso_Ridge.pdf'. One distinct file per contract; the provenance pointer for the row.
Spend category. Only 3 of the 6 categories used in Projects appear: 'Overhead - Budget Category' (30 rows), 'Plant large projects' (7) and 'PFAS' (3).

The gap as a percentage of the most recent budget plan, stored as the percentage number itself (58.3 means 58.3%), not a fraction. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load. The original held it as '58.3%'.
Total Budget Working USD minus Most Recent Budget Plan USD: the absolute budget overrun this table exists to surface. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
Latest approved budget-plan amount. Same measure as Projects.'Most Recent Budget Plan'. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
Capital project the exposure row covers. 40 distinct codes, predominantly overhead pseudo-projects (OVERHEAD4_670, OVERHEAD1_675). Joins to Projects.'Project Code'.
Descriptive project name, generally '<Project Code>-<category>' (e.g. 'OVERHEAD4_670-Overhead Projects'). One per row.
Ordinal position of the project in the budget-exposure ranking. 40 distinct values, neither contiguous nor in row order, so this table is a filtered slice of a larger ranking.
Operating region: Shared Services Division (12 rows), Eastmoor Region (9), Northvale Region (9), Cascadia Region (5), Lakeshore Region (5).
Current working total budget. Same measure as Projects.'Total Budget Working'. Rebuilt 2026-09-17 from the original header-less load.
The currently active budget-plan amount in whole dollars (INTEGER, so directly usable in arithmetic, unlike the FY columns). Null on 307 rows.

Whether the project is approved. True on 3,564 rows, False on 732 (every 'In Planning' project), and NULL on 204 -- the overhead rows, where approval does not apply. Treat NULL as 'not applicable', not as 'unknown'.
Asset type the spend lands on: Water Network (1,877), Water Treatment (1,822), Water Customer service lines (597), Overheads (204). No nulls.

Asset risk rating, already cleaned/normalised upstream: 'Tolerable Risk' (1,509), 'Not Applicable ARS' (1,265), 'Not Evaluated ARS' (917), 'Intolerable Risk' (809). No nulls -- the two 'Not ...' values encode absence of a rating rather than NULL.

Capital spend category, no nulls: Plant large projects (2,183), PFAS (749), Network blankets (714), Lead Capex Budget Category (443), Network common projects (207), Overhead - Budget Category (204). See also 'Budget Category 2' and 'High-Level Category', which are alternate roll-ups of the same split.
Alternate roll-up of 'Budget Category', identical to it except that 'PFAS' is spelled out as 'Federal PFAS Program'. Six values, no nulls.
Status of the budget plan: 'Active' (3,561) or 'Inactive' (732, matching the In Planning projects). Null on 207 rows.
Year-to-date budget for the current fiscal year, in US dollars. NULL on 732 rows. Converted from the source display string ('$4,100,463 ', '-' for none) to NUMERIC on 2026-09-17.
Operating business unit, formatted '<number> - <name>' (e.g. '690 - Dunmoor East'). 16 values, no nulls. The number matches the numeric suffix of the structured Project Codes.

Whether the project's scope or timing is considered optimisable when balancing the capital plan. True on 554 rows, False on 1,064, and NULL on 2,882 -- the flag has been assessed for barely a third of the portfolio, so do not read NULL as False.
Capital prioritisation tier, INTEGER 1-4, no nulls. Heavily skewed: 1 on 3,896 rows, 4 on 436, 2 on 136, 3 on 32 -- so level 1 is the default rather than a discriminating signal.

Regulatory or contractual obligation forcing the spend: 'Mandated by Government Agency' (2,215), 'No compliance constraint' (1,725), 'Committed to Third Party' (560). No nulls. The two non-'No' values mark work that cannot simply be deferred.

Cost-recovery treatment and customer impact: 'No Surcharge' (1,758), 'Surcharge DSIC' (1,107), 'Surcharge SIC' (976), 'Surcharge other' (659). DSIC/SIC are infrastructure surcharge mechanisms that let the spend be recovered between rate cases.

Project end date. Only 11 distinct values, all 31 December year-ends from 2026 to 2032 plus '2050-12-31' on 1,157 rows -- that far date is a sentinel for open-ended work, not a real schedule, and will distort any duration metric left unfiltered.
Projected date the completed asset enters service. Null on 897 rows, and '2026-01-01' on 888 more, which reads as a default rather than a real estimate. Also carried in the In_Service_Dates table.

Actual spend in fiscal year 2023, in US dollars. NULL on 2,535 rows -- most projects did not exist or had no spend that year. Converted from the source display string ('$4,100,463 ', '-' for none) to NUMERIC on 2026-09-17.

Actual spend in fiscal year 2026, the current year, in US dollars. NULL on 732 rows. Converted from the source display string ('$4,100,463 ', '-' for none) to NUMERIC on 2026-09-17.

properties.rationale: Change_Orders carries its own Project Code column, so this can be modeled as a direct two-table FK rather than hopping through Contracts — useful in BigQuery/BI tools that only support pairwise relationships, and convenient for "total change-order exposure per project" rollups without an extra join. This is a denormalized shortcut, not the authoritative lineage — the authoritative path is Change_Orders.Contract ID → Contracts.Contract ID → Contracts.Project Code, which is enforced by R1 + R2. In the sampled data, Change_Orders.Project Code always agrees with the Project Code on the matching Contract ID in Contracts, but this pair should be spot-checked periodically so the two paths don't silently drift apart.

Tracks contract value creep and schedule slippage. Each change order carries an Amount ($), a Revised price ($), and Days added, so this relationship drives contract cost-control reporting (Price at award → Price as adjusted) and lets project controls justify budget deviations with the underlying scope-change narrative.

A capital project is typically delivered through multiple procurement packages (e.g., civil, electrical, piping, services) rather than a single contract. This relationship lets finance/PMO roll up total contracted value, executed dates, and counterparties to the project level for portfolio reporting, and lets legal/procurement trace every contract instrument back to the funding project.

Exposure is a derived reporting extract — the Top‑40 projects ranked by budget gap (Gap ($)/Gap (%) = Total Budget Working − Most Recent Budget Plan) — not an independently maintained entity. In a data model this should be built as a view/mart on top of Projects (computing Gap and Rank), rather than a separately loaded fact table, to avoid the two figures drifting out of sync when Projects is refreshed.

story_group.story:
Northline manages a capital portfolio of 4,500 projects with $113 billion in authorized spending across fiscal years 2023 through 2032. The Projects table is the authoritative register for every project—one row per project code—and holds the complete financial picture: budget, forecast, and actual spend by fiscal year, together with project classification, phase, approval status, and schedule. Each project carries its active budget plan (the currently authorized amount in whole dollars), its most recent budget plan (the latest version, whether activated or not), and its inception-to-date actuals drawn from the accounting system. The FY26 Working Forecast is the live spending forecast for the current fiscal year; the FY26 Forecast 3+9 checkpoint (3 months of actuals plus 9 months of forecast) is the only quarterly re-forecast currently populated—the 6+6 and 9+3 checkpoints are unpopulated. The MTP2026_v3 columns hold the frozen baseline from the 2026 Mid-Term Plan, against which working budgets are compared to detect baseline movement. Inception-to-date actuals are also carried by fiscal year: FY25 ITD Actuals shows spend as of the end of FY25, while FY26 Actuals shows current-year spend. Most projects show no variance against their current approved budget because the approved amount was revised to absorb the variance, and the original commitment is reachable only by comparing current working budget to the MTP2026_v3 baseline—without that comparison visible on a standard report, the original overrun is invisible. Projects are classified by budget category (Plant large projects, PFAS, Network blankets, Lead Capex, Network common projects, Overhead), programme affiliation (Federal PFAS Program, Lead Program, or no programme), asset class (Water Network, Water Treatment, Water Customer service lines, or Overheads), compliance driver (Mandated by Government Agency, Committed to Third Party, or no constraint), and risk assessment. A project's lifecycle phase is one of In Planning, In Development, or In Delivery. Approval status distinguishes between projects that have been through the WIN capital approval process (marked by an approval level from 01 to 05 and an approval date) and those that have not; 1,155 of the 4,500 have been formally approved through WIN, while 732 are still in the planning phase and have no active budget plan. The Projects table also carries estimated in-service date and project start and end dates—though the end date is often the sentinel value 2050-12-31 for open-ended work, which will distort any duration calculation left unfiltered.

Contracts executed to deliver project scope are tracked separately, one row per contract ID. A single project is typically delivered through multiple procurement packages—separate contracts for civil work, engineering, electrical, supply, and services—so the relationship between Projects and Contracts is one-to-many. Each contract carries the counterparty name, the legal instrument type (Construction Agreement, Owner-Engineer Agreement, Equipment Supply Agreement, and others), and the standard EJCDC form it is based on. The contract price at award is recorded in Price At Award USD; the current price after all executed change orders is in Price As Adjusted USD. On the 15 contracts with no change orders, these two figures are identical; where change orders exist, the Net Change Orders USD column shows the cumulative movement from award to present. The source contract PDF is recorded as the provenance pointer.

Change orders—formal modifications to contract price and schedule—are tracked as one row per change order issued, keyed by the pair (Contract ID, Change Order number). Change Orders carries both the Project Code directly and the Contract ID, so the relationship to a project can be modeled either as a direct two-table link or by hopping through Contracts; the two paths always agree in the current data, but they should be spot-checked periodically so they do not silently drift. Each change order records its dollar amount (negative amounts are credits), the revised contract price once the order is applied, calendar days added to the contract schedule, and the basis—free-text justification extracted from the source change-order document that explains whether the change was due to differing site conditions, owner-caused delay, quantity reconciliation, or negotiated credits. This narrative is essential for rate-case defense and internal cost-growth justification, but it lives only in these extracted fields and nowhere else; the original documents are the source of record.

The Exposure table is a derived reporting extract, not an independently maintained entity—it ranks the top 40 projects by budget gap and is meant to serve as a prioritized watch list for finance and PMO leadership. Each row carries the gap between that project's most recent budget plan and its current working budget, expressed both in dollars and as a percentage of the most recent plan. Exposure should be built as a view computed from Projects rather than a separately loaded table, to ensure the two figures do not diverge when Projects is refreshed.

The In_Service_Dates table tracks when each project's asset is or is expected to be placed into service—the trigger for moving spend from construction-in-progress to a depreciable fixed asset, and the signal for rate-case timing. One row carries one project, though the table includes 260 legacy project codes that have no matching row in the current Projects table and will be silently dropped by an inner join. The estimated in-service date is carried here and also redundantly in Projects; the logical in-service date is held as a constant 2026-12-31 across all rows in this extract, so it conveys no per-project information. The In_Service_Dates table flags records marked "NEEDS TO BE UPDATED"—815 of 3,770 rows—but the condition it flags is undocumented, and the flag should be treated as provisional until that meaning is clarified.

Nothing in these tables records the reason a project's estimate at completion moved, the stage of the contracting cycle where capital is stalling, or which movements have a documented explanation versus which are unexplained—those narratives and stage-gates live in documents, email, and the heads of project managers. No table carries the approval history showing who approved each baseline revision and when, or the change-order justifications in their original form—only the extracted narrative from the change-order documents is present. The data does not distinguish between scope growth, cost escalation, schedule slip, and estimate error as drivers of overruns, nor does it record contractor performance or the aging profile of construction-in-progress. Without explicit linkage to the ledger, procurement system, and accrual records held in other systems, these tables cannot answer which actuals lack a matching commitment, which commitments exceed their authorization, or what accrued cost still has no invoice behind it—those reconciliations require joins outside this schema.

grain.Exposure: one row per project in the top 40 budget-gap ranking
grain.Projects: one row per project code (4,500 projects)
grain.Contracts: one row per Contract ID (one project can have multiple contracts for different scope packages)
grain.Change_Orders: one row per (Contract ID, Change Order number) pair
grain.In_Service_Dates: one row per project's in-service tracking record (includes 260 legacy codes no longer in Projects)

uncertainties: The exact cardinality of the Contracts → Change_Orders relationship: while it is stated that one contract can have multiple change orders, the distinctness cannot be confirmed without sample data statistics.
The exact cardinality of Projects → Contracts: while 'one-to-many' is declared, the distinctness of Contract ID relative to Project Code is not provided.

The semantics of the 'Basis' field in Change_Orders: the story says it contains 'free-text justification extracted from the source change-order document', but whether it is a fully-extracted narrative or a category label is ambiguous.
The full scope of what 'NEEDS TO BE UPDATED' flag in In_Service_Dates means: the story acknowledges this is 'undocumented' and provisional.
Whether all 260 legacy project codes in In_Service_Dates that lack a match in Projects represent historical projects or data quality issues.

Whether the 'Basis' narrative in Change_Orders is stored as raw free-text or if there is any structured categorization (differing site conditions, owner-caused delay, etc. appear to be exemplars rather than codes).

The relationship between Projects.Estimated_In_Service_Date (which is nullable and sometimes 2026-01-01 as a placeholder) and In_Service_Dates.Estimated_In_Service_Date: whether they always agree or are independently maintained.
Whether the two paths (Project → Change_Orders direct vs. Project → Contracts → Change_Orders) have been formally reconciled or only verified in the current sample.
